messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh was fifty-eight, a widower who had spent thirty years working the waters off the coast of Maine, and he could still feel the exact instant the truck crossed the double line. He had been driving home from the marina with his wife, Anjali, in the passenger seat—she had just brought him lunch—when a pickup drifted into their lane. He remembered the sound, the way the world folded, and then the long silence that followed, broken only by the faint crackle of the radio as he lay pinned, unable to move his legs, watching helplessly while her hand slipped from his. Anjali died at the scene. Rajesh survived with two broken ribs and a shattered pelvis, but the doctors said his heart had stopped once on the operating table. That was eighteen months ago. He still could not describe what happened aloud; whenever he tried, the words dissolved in his throat, and the memory flashed back with the same raw terror—the crushing metal, the smell of gasoline, the numb certainty that he was already dead. The event felt present, not past, as though he were still trapped in that moment, and the panic that surged through him each time was as acute as the original.

In the months that followed, Rajesh returned to fishing because he needed the income, but the ocean, which had once been his comfort, became a place of unrelenting vigilance. He constantly scanned the deck for any sign of danger—a loose line, a shifting crate, an unusual pattern on the water. At home, the silence of the empty house made his heart race; he had come to believe that quiet meant something dreadful was about to happen, so he kept the radio on at all hours, even while he slept. Strangers were the worst. When a customer at the dock asked for his catch or a new deckhand introduced himself, Rajesh felt a cold knot in his stomach. He had started to distrust everyone—people were not what they seemed, and in his mind, any unfamiliar face could be the driver of that truck, someone whose carelessness would shatter another life. These encounters not only reinforced his suspicion of others but also dragged the accident memory to the surface: a stranger’s voice would become Anjali’s last whisper, and he would taste the grit of shattered windshield glass.

The distrust and the flashbacks fed each other. Every time the memory erupted—often when he saw a car that had been in a collision, or when someone casually mentioned losing a loved one—Rajesh felt the ground drop from under him. He no longer knew who he was. The man who had fixed nets, told jokes at the bait shop, and made Anjali laugh seemed like a stranger. Even his own body felt unreliable: his ribs ached unpredictably, and he sometimes lost sensation in his legs, which convinced him that another collapse was imminent. These appraisals kept his threat system on high alert. At the supermarket, he would find himself backing into a corner to keep all shoppers in view; at the dock, he would refuse help from anyone he did not know, certain that an unguarded moment would cost him everything. The hypervigilance, in turn, made the memory more vivid. When he was most on guard, the accident would replay in full sensory detail—the screech, the impact, the wet warmth on his face—and the loop would tighten again. After these vivid intrusions, even the most ordinary sights—a truck in his rearview mirror, a sudden brake light—felt like warnings he could not afford to ignore.

His fishing routine began to shrink. He avoided the main pier where tourists gathered, and he took only short trips close to shore, even though the best catches were farther out. One afternoon, a young woman on the dock was sobbing on her phone, saying over and over, “He’s gone, he’s gone,” and Rajesh had to drop his gear and walk away, his hands trembling so violently that he could not hold his coffee. The loss theme was unbearable because it confirmed his own appraisal that the world was a place where people disappear without warning. After that, he stopped going to the weekly fishermen’s meeting. His crew noticed his distance; one of them told the harbormaster that Rajesh had become “spooked.” He did not explain. He only became more alert at home, checking the locks twice, listening for noises that might herald another catastrophe.

What finally brought Rajesh to a clinic was a morning last month when a dense fog settled over the harbor. The unusual silence—no gulls, no engine hum—sent him into a full panic. He was certain something terrible was about to happen, and he locked himself in his truck, sobbing, until a fellow fisherman knocked on the window. Feeling this afraid all the time, he had come to believe that he was no longer the kind of person who could live without constant dread, that this was simply who he had become. That night, he could not find words to tell his daughter what was wrong. He sat in the dark, the memory of the crash as present as the chair beneath him, and he thought: I don’t know who I am anymore. The next day, he called a number a doctor had given him months ago. He was terrified that if he let the memory surface fully, it would drown him, but he was also desperate to stop feeling like a stranger in his own life.
